specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe some of the biological factors affecting levels of food security.
Food security is having enough food to feed a population.

Biological factors which are threatening food security include: the increasing birth rate has threatened food security in some countries; changing diets in developed countries means scarce food resources are transported around the world; new pests and pathogens that affect farming; environmental changes that affect food production, such as widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail; the cost of agricultural inputs; conflicts that have arisen in some parts of the world which affect the availability of water or food.
Sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.

The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. This can be done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings.
Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth.
Fish stocks in the oceans are declining. It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas.
Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level.
Students should be able to describe and explain some possible biotechnical and agricultural solutions, including genetic modification, to the demands of the growing human population.
Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food.

The fungus Fusarium is useful for producing mycoprotein, a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.
A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. When harvested and purified this is used to treat people with diabetes.
GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value such as golden rice.

concepts.definition: Having enough food to feed a population.

Factors that reduce the amount of food available to a population. They include: the increasing birth rate, which has threatened food security in some countries; changing diets in developed countries, which means scarce food resources are transported around the world; new pests and pathogens that affect farming; environmental changes that affect food production, such as widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail; the cost of agricultural inputs; and conflicts that have arisen in some parts of the world which affect the availability of water or food.
Producing food in ways that can be continued into the future without the supply running out. Sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.

concepts.term: Restricting energy transfer from food animals
concepts.definition: The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. This can be done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings, so that more of the energy in their food is used for growth.

concepts.term: High protein foods in animal feed
concepts.definition: Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth, which improves the efficiency of food production.
Fish stocks in the oceans are declining. It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues, or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas.

concepts.term: Fishing quotas and control of net size
concepts.definition: Two methods used to conserve fish stocks at a sustainable level. A fishing quota is a limit on the mass or number of a species that may be caught. Controlling net size, by setting a minimum mesh size, allows young fish to escape so that breeding continues.
Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food, providing a source of protein for a growing human population.
A protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians, produced using the fungus Fusarium. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.

concepts.term: Human insulin from a genetically modified bacterium
concepts.definition: A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. When harvested and purified this is used to treat people with diabetes.

misconceptions.question: What does food security mean?
misconceptions.correct: Food security is having enough food to feed a population.
misconceptions.misconception: Food security means a country growing all of its own food inside its own borders, so any country that imports food does not have food security.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'security' suggests self-defence and independence, and students hear about countries 'relying on imports' in the news, so they assume the measure is where the food is grown rather than whether there is enough of it.
misconceptions.correction: Food security is having enough food to feed a population. Where the food is produced is not part of the definition; changing diets in developed countries means scarce food resources are transported around the world, and this is listed as a factor affecting food security, not as the definition of it.

misconceptions.question: Which kinds of factor are threatening food security?
misconceptions.correct: Biological factors threatening food security include the increasing birth rate, changing diets in developed countries, new pests and pathogens, environmental changes such as failed rains, the cost of agricultural inputs, and conflicts affecting the availability of water or food.
misconceptions.misconception: Food security is only threatened by environmental changes such as rains failing, because famine is what causes people to go short of food.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Images of drought and famine dominate media coverage of food shortages, so students treat environmental change as the single cause and overlook the other factors listed in the specification.
misconceptions.correction: Environmental changes that affect food production, such as widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail, are only one of the biological factors listed. The increasing birth rate, changing diets in developed countries, new pests and pathogens that affect farming, the cost of agricultural inputs, and conflicts that affect the availability of water or food all threaten food security as well.

misconceptions.question: Is food security the same thing as sustainable food production?
misconceptions.correct: Food security is having enough food to feed a population; separately, sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: Food security means producing food in a way that does not damage the environment, so a country with environmentally friendly farming automatically has food security.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two ideas appear in the same specification point and are often taught in the same lesson, so students merge them into a single definition.
misconceptions.correction: Food security is having enough food to feed a population. Sustainability is a separate requirement: sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth, so that food production can continue in the future.

misconceptions.question: How is energy transfer from food animals to the environment restricted?
misconceptions.correct: By limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is improved by giving food animals plenty of room to move and by keeping them in cool surroundings, because a cool animal that exercises uses less energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that exercise is healthy and that being hot is uncomfortable, so they assume free movement and cool conditions must be the efficient option; they also forget that a mammal in cold surroundings transfers more energy to the environment while keeping its body temperature constant.
misconceptions.correction: The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. This can be done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings, so less of the energy in their food is transferred to the environment and more is available for growth.

misconceptions.question: Why are some food animals fed high protein foods?
misconceptions.correct: Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth.
misconceptions.misconception: High protein foods are given to food animals to supply them with extra energy for movement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet protein in the diet alongside carbohydrate and lipid and remember that food releases energy, so they treat every extra nutrient as an energy supply rather than as raw material for new tissue.
misconceptions.correction: Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth. The protein is used for growth, which raises the efficiency of food production; energy transfer to the environment is restricted separately by limiting movement and controlling the temperature of the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: Do fish stocks need to be managed, or will they recover on their own?
misconceptions.correct: It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas.
misconceptions.misconception: Fish stocks recover on their own however many fish are caught, because fish lay very large numbers of eggs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that fish produce huge numbers of eggs and that the oceans are vast, so they assume the population can replace itself at any level of fishing.
misconceptions.correction: Fish stocks in the oceans are declining. It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues, or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas, so limits on fishing are needed.

misconceptions.question: How does controlling net size help to conserve fish stocks?
misconceptions.correct: Control of net size, along with fishing quotas, conserves fish stocks at a sustainable level; a larger mesh size allows young fish to escape so that breeding continues.
misconceptions.misconception: Using nets with a smaller mesh size conserves fish stocks, because smaller nets catch fewer fish.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'small net' as 'small catch' and picture the overall size of the net rather than the size of the holes in the mesh.
misconceptions.correction: Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level. A larger mesh size lets young fish pass through the net so they survive to breed, maintaining stocks at a level where breeding continues.

misconceptions.question: Which organism produces mycoprotein, and in what conditions is it grown?
misconceptions.correct: The fungus Fusarium produces mycoprotein, and it is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Mycoprotein is produced by bacteria grown in anaerobic conditions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet bacteria far more often than fungi in biotechnology examples, and they associate industrial vats of microorganisms with anaerobic fermentation such as brewing.
misconceptions.correction: The fungus Fusarium is useful for producing mycoprotein, a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.

misconceptions.question: How does a genetically modified bacterium help to treat people with diabetes?
misconceptions.correct: The genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin, which is harvested and purified before being used to treat people with diabetes.
misconceptions.misconception: People with diabetes are treated by taking the genetically modified bacteria themselves, so that the bacteria make insulin inside the patient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that some microorganisms live in the human gut and hear about 'good bacteria' in foods, so they assume the modified bacterium is delivered into the body rather than used as a factory outside it.
misconceptions.correction: A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. When harvested and purified this is used to treat people with diabetes; it is the insulin, not the bacterium, that is given to the patient.

misconceptions.question: What can genetically modified crops provide?
misconceptions.correct: GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value such as golden rice.
misconceptions.misconception: Genetically modified crops can only increase the amount of food produced; they cannot change how nutritious the food is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: GM crops are usually introduced through examples of higher yield and pest resistance, so students remember quantity and never meet an example where the nutritional value of the food itself is changed.
misconceptions.correction: GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value, such as golden rice, so genetic modification can change the quality of the food as well as the quantity produced.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by food security?

options.text: Growing a country's food within its borders.
options.rationale: A student who believes food security means self-sufficiency picks the option about growing food inside the country. Where food is produced is not part of the definition; changing diets in developed countries means scarce food resources are transported around the world, and imported food still feeds a population.

options.text: Storing enough food to survive any famine.
options.rationale: A student who believes only environmental changes such as failed rains threaten food security reduces the whole idea to famine relief. Famine is one example of an environmental change affecting food production, not the meaning of food security.

options.text: Having enough food to feed a population.
options.rationale: Food security is having enough food to feed a population, which is exactly what this option states.

options.text: Producing food without damaging habitats.
options.rationale: A student who treats food security and sustainability as the same idea chooses the environmental option. Sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth, but that is a separate requirement from having enough food to feed a population.

mcqs.stem: A new insect pest spreads into a country and destroys much of its wheat crop. Which biological factor affecting food security does this describe?

options.text: New pests and pathogens that affect farming.
options.rationale: An insect pest that has newly spread into the country and reduced the harvest is an example of new pests and pathogens that affect farming, one of the biological factors threatening food security.

options.text: An increasing birth rate in some countries.
options.rationale: A student who believes food security is about a country producing enough for its own people blames a growing number of mouths to feed. The increasing birth rate is a listed factor, but nothing in this situation describes a change in population size; the crop was destroyed by an organism.

options.text: Environmental change such as rains failing.
options.rationale: A student who believes only environmental changes such as failed rains threaten food security defaults to this option. Environmental change is a separate listed factor; here the cause is a living organism attacking the crop, not a change in climate or rainfall.

options.text: Changing diets in the developed countries.
options.rationale: A student who confuses food security with sustainability picks the option about diets, because transporting food around the world sounds unsustainable. Changing diets in developed countries is a listed factor, but the shortage described here is caused by the pest destroying the crop.

mcqs.stem: A farmer rears animals for meat indoors. Which change would improve the efficiency of food production?

options.text: Give them more space in which to move around.
options.rationale: A student who thinks free movement is the efficient option chooses more space. Movement transfers energy from the animals to the environment, so allowing more movement leaves less of the energy in their food available for growth.

options.text: Keep them in cool, well ventilated buildings.
options.rationale: A student who thinks cool surroundings save energy chooses this. In cool surroundings the animals transfer more energy to the environment while keeping their body temperature constant, so efficiency falls; the temperature of their surroundings should be controlled.

options.text: Feed them a diet that is lower in protein.
options.rationale: A student who thinks protein is fed as an energy supply assumes that less protein means less energy wasted. Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth, so lowering the protein in the diet would reduce growth.

options.text: Limit movement and control the temperature.
options.rationale: The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment, and this is done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings.

mcqs.stem: Why are some food animals fed high protein foods?

options.text: To increase their rate of growth.
options.rationale: Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth, which improves the efficiency of food production.

options.text: To give them energy for movement.
options.rationale: A student who treats protein as an energy supply picks this. High protein foods are fed to increase growth; energy transfer to the environment is reduced by limiting movement, not by fuelling it.

options.text: To keep their surroundings warmer.
options.rationale: A student who muddles the two ways of improving efficiency links the feed to temperature. Controlling the temperature of the surroundings is a separate method; the high protein food is fed to increase growth.

options.text: To reduce the food that they eat.
options.rationale: A student who thinks protein simply supplies energy assumes a richer feed means the animal needs less of it. The purpose stated in the specification is to increase growth.

mcqs.stem: Fish stocks in one area of ocean are declining. Which action would help to conserve the stocks at a sustainable level?

options.text: Remove quotas and keep the net size the same.
options.rationale: A student who believes stocks recover on their own sees no need for limits. Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level, so removing quotas would let stocks fall further.

options.text: Use fishing quotas and control the net size.
options.rationale: Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level, maintaining stocks at a level where breeding continues.

options.text: Use small mesh nets to catch the young fish.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a smaller mesh means a smaller catch picks this. A small mesh traps young fish before they have bred, so stocks are no longer maintained at a level where breeding continues.

options.text: Keep fishing until the stocks begin to fall.
options.rationale: A student who believes stocks always bounce back is willing to wait for a fall before acting. Stocks must be maintained at a level where breeding continues, or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas.

mcqs.stem: Mycoprotein is a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. How is it produced?

options.text: Bacteria are grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
options.rationale: A student who believes mycoprotein comes from bacteria picks the right conditions but the wrong organism. Mycoprotein is produced using the fungus Fusarium.

options.text: Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in anaerobic conditions.
options.rationale: A student who associates large vats of microorganisms with anaerobic fermentation picks the right organism but the wrong conditions. The fungus is grown in aerobic conditions.

options.text: Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
options.rationale: The fungus Fusarium is useful for producing mycoprotein. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.

options.text: Yeast is grown on glucose syrup, in anaerobic conditions.
options.rationale: A student holding the belief that mycoprotein comes from an anaerobic culture chooses the microorganism they most often meet in anaerobic conditions. Mycoprotein is produced using Fusarium grown in aerobic conditions.

mcqs.stem: Golden rice is a genetically modified crop. How can GM crops help to meet the demands of the growing human population?

options.text: By providing medicines inside the food eaten.
options.rationale: A student who believes genetically modified organisms are swallowed so that they work inside the body applies the same idea to crops. In the specification example, a genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin, which is harvested and purified before use; GM crops provide food, not medicine inside the food.

options.text: By providing more food, not improved nutrition.
options.rationale: A student who believes genetic modification can only raise yield rules out any change in quality. GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value, such as golden rice.

options.text: By providing food grown from cultured fungi.
options.rationale: A student who mixes up the biotechnology examples attributes the crop to fungal culture. Growing the fungus Fusarium on glucose syrup produces mycoprotein; a GM crop such as golden rice is a plant grown in fields.

options.text: By providing more food or improved nutrition.
options.rationale: GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value such as golden rice, which is one biotechnical and agricultural solution to the demands of the growing human population.
